verses.text: Yahweh sent Nathan to David. He came to him, and said to him, “There were two men in one city; the one rich, and the other poor.
The rich man had very many flocks and herds,

but the poor man had nothing, except one little ewe lamb, which he had bought and raised. It grew up together with him, and with his children. It ate of his own food, drank of his own cup, and lay in his bosom, and was like a daughter to him.

A traveler came to the rich man, and he spared to take of his own flock and of his own herd, to prepare for the wayfaring man who had come to him, but took the poor man’s lamb, and prepared it for the man who had come to him.”
David’s anger burned hot against the man, and he said to Nathan, “As Yahweh lives, the man who has done this deserves to die!
He must restore the lamb fourfold, because he did this thing, and because he had no pity!”
Nathan said to David, “You are the man. This is what Yahweh, the God of Israel, says: ‘I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you out of the hand of Saul.

I gave you your master’s house, and your master’s wives into your bosom, and gave you the house of Israel and of Judah; and if that would have been too little, I would have added to you many more such things.

Why have you despised Yahweh’s word, to do that which is evil in his sight? You have struck Uriah the Hittite with the sword, and have taken his wife to be your wife, and have slain him with the sword of the children of Ammon.
Now therefore the sword will never depart from your house, because you have despised me, and have taken Uriah the Hittite’s wife to be your wife.’

“This is what Yahweh says: ‘Behold, I will raise up evil against you out of your own house; and I will take your wives before your eyes, and give them to your neighbor, and he will lie with your wives in the sight of this sun.
For you did this secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel, and before the sun.’”
David said to Nathan, “I have sinned against Yahweh.” Nathan said to David, “Yahweh also has put away your sin. You will not die.
However, because by this deed you have given great occasion to Yahweh’s enemies to blaspheme, the child also who is born to you will surely die.”
Nathan departed to his house. Yahweh struck the child that Uriah’s wife bore to David, and it was very sick.
David therefore begged God for the child; and David fasted, and went in, and lay all night on the ground.
The elders of his house arose beside him, to raise him up from the earth: but he would not, and he didn’t eat bread with them.

On the seventh day, the child died. David’s servants were afraid to tell him that the child was dead, for they said, “Behold, while the child was yet alive, we spoke to him, and he didn’t listen to our voice. How will he then harm himself, if we tell him that the child is dead?”
But when David saw that his servants were whispering together, David perceived that the child was dead; and David said to his servants, “Is the child dead?” They said, “He is dead.”

Then David arose from the earth, and washed, and anointed himself, and changed his clothing; and he came into Yahweh’s house, and worshiped. Then he came to his own house; and when he requested, they set bread before him, and he ate.
Then his servants said to him, “What is this that you have done? You fasted and wept for the child while he was alive, but when the child was dead, you rose up and ate bread.”
He said, “While the child was yet alive, I fasted and wept; for I said, ‘Who knows whether Yahweh will not be gracious to me, that the child may live?’
But now he is dead, why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I will go to him, but he will not return to me.”
David comforted Bathsheba his wife, and went in to her, and lay with her. She bore a son, and he called his name Solomon. Yahweh loved him;
and he sent by the hand of Nathan the prophet, and he named him Jedidiah,  for Yahweh’s sake.
Now Joab fought against Rabbah of the children of Ammon, and took the royal city.
Joab sent messengers to David, and said, “I have fought against Rabbah. Yes, I have taken the city of waters.
Now therefore gather the rest of the people together, and encamp against the city, and take it; lest I take the city, and it be called by my name.”
David gathered all the people together, and went to Rabbah, and fought against it, and took it.

He took the crown of their king from off his head; and its weight was a talent  of gold, and in it were precious stones; and it was set on David’s head. He brought a great quantity of plunder out of the city.

He brought out the people who were in it, and put them under saws, under iron picks, under axes of iron, and made them pass through the brick kiln; and he did so to all the cities of the children of Ammon. Then David and all the people returned to Jerusalem.

footnotes.content: A prophet arrives with a parable—a teacher's old trick, and Nathan knows his king. David doesn't yet realize he's the poor man in his own story, nor that Yahweh sees what he thought was hidden. Sometimes we need a mirror dressed up as a neighbor's trouble.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The rich man's plenty—flocks and herds without number—speaks of a kind of blindness. When we have so much, the taking of one small thing becomes almost reflex, a shadow crime we don't see as sin. I've noticed this too in my own heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A ewe lamb loved like a daughter, eating from a man's own plate, lying in his bosom—this is the voice of love and tenderness. The poor man's one treasure is also his companion, his hope made small. When we recognize what love looks like, we know what cruelty steals.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The rich man has everything but will not spare even one small thing for a guest. Instead, he takes the poor man's lamb—the only living warmth the poor man had. This is not hunger; this is the hunger of a man who already has much but wants to keep others small.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David's anger burns hot and swift—he sees clear injustice and judges it without mercy. He is righteous in his wrath, and he means it. How little he knows, in this moment, that he is pronouncing judgment on himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fourfold restitution—the law of Exodus, spoken in David's own mouth. He calls for justice and payment, not knowing he is writing his own sentence. The words we speak in righteous anger have a way of circling back to us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nathan speaks the hardest words a prophet can speak: 'You are the man.' No softer preamble, no shield of ceremony—just the plain truth, and a reminder of grace. Yahweh anointed David, delivered him from Saul, raised him from nothing. This is why the fall matters so much.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh gave and gave—the house of David's master, the wives, all Israel and Judah, and He would have given even more. The bounty was real. And yet David looked at what he had and wanted what belonged to another. More shame, not less, when the giver has been so generous.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The indictment is clean and sharp: despised Yahweh's word, struck down an innocent man, took his wife. David did this, not through ignorance or weakness, but by choice—and worse, by the hands of others while pretending innocence. The layers of the sin are named without mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sword will never depart from your house—a sentence that will haunt David's whole reign. From this moment forward, his household is marked by violence, the wages of his own hidden deed. Mercy will come, but not without a cost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Evil raised up out of his own house—his own children will turn his strength against him, his wives will be taken before his eyes as a sign to all Israel. What he did in secret, Yahweh will make public. There is a terrible justice here, and David will live to see it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: What was done in darkness will be exposed in the light—not just to David, but before all Israel and even in the sight of the sun itself. The secret is now the nation's knowledge, the shame is made common. There is no hiding from Yahweh.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David's confession is spare and true: 'I have sinned against Yahweh.' No excuse, no explanation—just the plain admission. And Nathan's reply is a doorway: 'Yahweh has put away your sin.' Forgiveness is real, though the consequences will be borne. This is how mercy looks when sin is truly seen and truly named.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sin carries weight beyond the sinner—by this deed David has given Yahweh's enemies occasion to blaspheme, and the child must die. The innocent pay a price for the guilty's choice. This truth is hard, but it teaches us how far sin reaches, and why we must guard our hearts so carefully.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The child becomes very sick—and David knows the weight of what he has heard. Nathan leaves, and the illness becomes the lived reality of judgment. A father waits, and a small life hangs in the balance as consequence made flesh.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David begs God for the child and fasts—he lies on the ground through the night, begging for mercy now that his eyes are open. The great king becomes small before Yahweh, pleading not for himself but for his son. This is the grief of a man who would trade everything he has for one small life.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The elders try to lift him up, to comfort him, but David will not rise. He lies on the ground in his sackcloth and ash, refusing the bread they offer. This is not pride; it is the depth of his mourning, a man who knows he has no right to ease or rest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: On the seventh day the child dies—the waiting is over, and David's worst fear is real. His servants fear to tell him, afraid he will harm himself when he hears the news. They have never seen their king so broken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David knows by watching his servants whisper—he reads the truth in their fear and in their eyes. He asks plainly, and they answer plainly, and in that moment something shifts in David's heart. The waiting is worse than the knowing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David rises from the earth, washes, anoints himself, changes his clothes, and goes to worship. Then he comes to his own house and eats bread. The man who lay on the ground through his son's illness now stands and returns to life. It is an act of faith, a strange mercy—he will see his son again, even if not in this world.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His servants are baffled—when the child lived, David fasted and wept, but now that the child is dead, he rises and eats? It seems backward, a betrayal of grief itself. They do not yet understand that David has learned something in that long night on the ground.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David explains: 'While the child was alive, I fasted and wept. Who knows whether Yahweh might be gracious?' He was pleading, hoping, leaving room for mercy. But now? Now there is only acceptance and the knowledge that he will join his son, not that his son will return to him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Can I bring him back? No. But I will go to him. These words hold both the depth of David's loss and the strange comfort of an older faith—the belief that death is not the end, only a separation that will be mended. A grieving father speaks, but also a man of hope.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David comforts Bathsheba—she also has grieved, and now he goes to her, and she conceives and bears a son. The child is called Solomon, and Yahweh loved him. From the ashes of judgment, a new life grows, and Yahweh's favor rests on him. Grace moves through generations.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nathan sends word to name the child Jedidiah—'beloved of Yahweh'—a secret name that speaks of grace received. The prophet who spoke judgment now speaks mercy. Solomon will be Yahweh's instrument of wisdom and peace, born from repentance and held in the palm of Yahweh's love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joab fights against Rabbah, the great city of Ammon—the king's business continues even as David grieves. War does not pause for a king's heart to heal; the work of the kingdom goes on.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joab sends word that the city of waters—the water supply—is now in his hands. He has taken the battle but holds back from taking the city itself, waiting for his king. A general's courtesy to the man who sent him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joab asks David to come and finish the work, lest the victory be claimed by Joab's name instead of the king's. There is politics here, the careful dance of power, but also deference—Joab knows his place and holds it for his king.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David gathers all the people and goes to Rabbah and takes it—the king returns to war, his strength renewed. From his chamber of grief he comes to the field of battle, and the kingdom's expansion continues under his hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He takes the crown from the king of Ammon and sets it on his own head—a talent of gold, set with precious stones. The plunder is great, and David's power is declared to all the nations. Yet this earthly crown means little beside what he has lost and what grace has restored.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David brings the people of the cities under subjection—the hard work of conquest and rule follows victory. The chapter closes with David returning to Jerusalem, a king hardened by judgment and softened by mercy, carrying both the weight and the blessing of what he has learned.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
